newsitem.title: USA: IMF to get mandate to promote free capital flows.
newsitem.headline: IMF to get mandate to promote free capital flows.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund's Interim Committee on Monday approved a plan to give the IMF a mandate to promote the free flow of capital worldwide.

But it failed to reach agreement on two other proposals -- an increase in the IMF's capital, or quotas, and an allocation of the Fund's artificial currency, the Special Drawing Right, to member nations.

"The Fund's articles (of agreement) should be amended to make the promotion of capital account liberalization a specific purpose of the Fund," the policy-making Interim Committee said in a statement issued after a day of talks.

But, in recognition of some unease among developing countries about the risks posed by such a move, the IMF panel said that nations should be given time to liberalize capital movements and be allowed to temporarily reimpose controls in times of crisis.
The IMF should be bold in its objective of liberalizing capital flows, but be cautious in implementing it, said Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt, who is chairman of the Interim Committee.
Maystadt also voiced hopes that the IMF would be able to reach agreement in coming months on an SDR allocation, despite its inability to do so on Monday.
"We did not succeed in closing the gap on SDRs," he told reporters. "All the issues have been settled except for the size," he added.

The panel was split over an allocation of anywhere from 20 billion to 22.4 billion SDRs, or $27.4 to $30.7 billion at current rates. The SDR allocation would be mainly aimed at giving Special Drawing Rights to about 40 member nations which presently do not have them.

In its statement, the Interim Committee asked the IMF board to finalize its work on an SDR issue as soon as possible and to report back in time for the next semi-annual meeting of the Fund and the World Bank, in September in Hong Kong.
The panel also made the same request to the board with respect to proposals to increase the IMF's capital.
Member nations have yet to agree on the size of a capital increase -- the range is from 35 to 60 percent -- or how it will be distributed.
